title: The Chokepoint Trap
gist: Farrell, Newman and Tan argue that the global fixation on economic chokepoints creates a collective security-dilemma-style trap: each state's effort to wield or defend against chokepoints provokes retaliation and imitation, making a fragmented, volatile world and eventually war more likely, with little prospect of a Cold War-style off-ramp.

insights.claim: Globalization produced proliferating chokepoints in supply chains, the dollar system and digital platforms, and governments now focus on chokepoint capabilities rather than strategy.
insights.speaker: Henry Farrell
insights.so_what: Economic interdependence is now treated as a vulnerability; expect more state intervention in supply chains and payments.
insights.quote: Policymakers used to ignore chokepoints. Now they have trouble seeing anything else.
insights.locator: Opening paragraph

insights.claim: The pursuit of chokepoint power creates a security dilemma in which one country's efforts to secure itself make others feel threatened and respond in kind, leaving everyone less safe.
insights.speaker: Henry Farrell
insights.so_what: Use the security-dilemma lens to anticipate tit-for-tat escalation in trade and tech controls.
insights.locator: The result is a familiar but dangerous dynamic

insights.claim: US efforts to hamstring Chinese technology firms led China to accelerate its own technology development, which in turn spurred American fears of Chinese domination, a self-perpetuating spiral.
insights.speaker: Henry Farrell
insights.so_what: Export controls on semiconductors tend to accelerate Chinese self-reliance, eroding US leverage over time.
insights.locator: The United States' efforts to hamstring Chinese technology firms

insights.claim: The trap is collective and hard to escape because any government that exercises restraint risks becoming a victim; the most likely outcome is a fragmented world with greater volatility and risk of economic shocks, cascading disruptions and even war.
insights.speaker: Henry Farrell
insights.so_what: Base case is persistent fragmentation and volatility, not a return to efficient globalization.
insights.locator: Escaping the chokepoint trap will be difficult

insights.claim: Economic policies are harder than military ones to classify as offensive or defensive, so actions such as China building up its semiconductor sector can be read as coercive capacity.
insights.speaker: Henry Farrell
insights.so_what: Industrial policy in strategic sectors will be read by rivals as a threat, inviting countermeasures.

insights.claim: Economic agencies such as central banks and commerce departments are weakly coordinated and do not speak with one voice, which worsens signaling ambiguity; this year's Treasury-Federal Reserve disagreements over bond yields illustrate visible conflict.
insights.speaker: Henry Farrell
insights.so_what: Institutional incoherence adds noise to US policy signals, including on bond yields.

insights.claim: Because states hold different chokepoints, proportional retaliation is hard: in April 2025 China answered US tariffs and chip export controls with rare-earth restrictions because it does not control the same semiconductor chokepoint.
insights.speaker: Henry Farrell
insights.so_what: Retaliation will arrive in unexpected sectors, widening the set of exposed industries.

insights.claim: In a world where everything is connected nearly everything can be considered a chokepoint; a bill introduced in the US Senate in 2025 and House in 2026 even identifies smart ovens and clothes dryers as potential security threats.
insights.speaker: Henry Farrell
insights.so_what: Security-driven restrictions can spread to mundane consumer goods.

insights.claim: After 9/11 the US systematically exploited the dollar system and global communications networks; a 2024 Washington Post analysis found the US was sanctioning people, properties or organizations in a third of all countries, and a former Commerce official said nobody in government is sure the strategy works.
insights.speaker: Henry Farrell
insights.so_what: Sanctions overuse invites hedging against dollar dependence.

insights.claim: China's shift to chokepoint tools was triggered by Snowden's 2013 revelations and the first Trump administration's campaigns against ZTE and Huawei, after which Xi Jinping's 'dual circulation' strategy and mirrored export-control and investment-screening regimes followed.
insights.speaker: Henry Farrell
insights.so_what: Chinese self-reliance and its own coercion toolkit are structural, not reversible by a deal.

insights.claim: After 'Liberation Day' tariffs in April 2025, China imposed rare-earth licensing, suggested its processing dominance gave it authority over the entire semiconductor supply chain, barred some dual-use exports to US defense contractors, sanctioned firms over Taiwan arms cooperation, and opened antitrust probes into Google, Nvidia and DuPont.
insights.speaker: Henry Farrell
insights.so_what: US tech names with China exposure can be targeted via antitrust and export tools.

insights.claim: China is building a 'blocking' regime to punish companies that comply with other countries' economic restrictions; foreign banks that follow US law on a sanctioned Chinese refinery could be sued in Chinese courts, and August 2026 rules bar Chinese firms from dealing with six supply-chain due-diligence and labor-rights organizations.
insights.speaker: Henry Farrell

insights.claim: Since 2020 countries have enacted on average seven times as many export restrictions per year as in 2010-2019, according to Global Trade Alert.
insights.speaker: Henry Farrell
insights.so_what: Quantifies the secular rise in trade restrictions; supports a regime of structurally higher trade friction.

insights.claim: Europe has built an anti-coercion instrument, an economic security strategy and a Chips Act 2.0 but has struggled to turn them into leverage, remains dependent on US technology and security guarantees, and has not used the instrument against the US.
insights.speaker: Henry Farrell

insights.speaker: Henry Farrell
insights.so_what: European auto supply chains are exposed to Chinese chip and component chokepoints.

insights.claim: Japan began preparing for Chinese coercion early, built a national rare-earth stockpile and made itself indispensable to US military supply chains, though it also used chokepoints against South Korea in 2019 on semiconductor chemicals.

insights.claim: Historical precedent for economic fears driving aggression: Nicholas Mulder's The Economic Weapon documents that in the 1930s Axis powers' fear of League of Nations sanctions led them to seize territory and resources before it was too late.
insights.speaker: Henry Farrell
insights.so_what: Economic-isolation fears have historically contributed to preemptive aggression.

insights.claim: Cold War-style restraint exists only in small examples, such as Singapore's supply agreements with Australia and New Zealand and the 2022 WTO commitment not to restrict food exports for the World Food Programme, and scaling it is hard.
insights.speaker: Henry Farrell
insights.so_what: Narrow assurance agreements are the realistic form of de-escalation.
